system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, morbid obesity, and a history of venous thrombosis was admitted for evaluation of persistent nausea and malaise. She had no abdominal pain or vomiting but reported a dry cough and night sweats. Initial concerns for infection led to a brief course of antibiotics, but imaging showed a chronic retrocardiac opacity unlikely to be infectious, and antibiotics were discontinued. Nausea was thought to be related to gastroesophageal reflux, and she was started on omeprazole. A sacral fungal rash with a fissure was identified and treated with topical ketoconazole. She remained stable, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing dialysis and outpatient follow-up for a breast mass, dermatology, and primary care. Her home medications, including warfarin, insulin, and constipation regimens, were continued.
problems: Other nonspecific abnormal finding of lung field
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Rash and other nonspecific skin eruption
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen

referred for a preoperative wire localization prior to surgical resection.

PROCEDURE:  The procedure, risks, and benefits were discussed with the patient
and written informed consent was obtained.  The patient's medications were
reviewed.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed using three patient
identifiers.

Using standard aseptic technique, and ___ cc of 1% Lidocaine for local

proximal stiffeners.

shows two new localizing wires in the right breast. The targets are located at
the proximal stiffeners of the wires.
The lesions are located in the inferior central and outer right breast.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

The procedure was performed by Dr. ___ and the attending
radiologist, Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. You’ve been admitted today because of the breast masses we’ve been monitoring. We’re here to get you ready for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thank you. I’ve been nervous about this. I still can’t feel the lumps myself, but I know they’ve grown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very common. Many women don’t feel breast masses even when they’re visible on imaging. The mammogram showed two areas that increased in size—from 9mm and 5mm to 14mm and 8mm—so we want to remove them to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my cousin had breast cancer, so I’m worried it might be the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Family history does increase risk, but we won’t know for sure until after the surgery and pathology. Right now, we’re treating this as suspicious, which is why we’re moving forward with the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also take Coumadin for blood clots. I read that might be a problem with surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because you’re on long-term anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis, we need to temporarily stop Coumadin and switch to a heparin drip. That’s called a ‘heparin bridge.’ It keeps your blood thin but can be reversed quickly before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So I’m on heparin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we started the heparin drip this afternoon. We’re monitoring your PTT to make sure it’s in the right range—between 60 and 80. Your INR was 2.6 earlier, which is a bit high for surgery, so holding Coumadin was the right move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about dialysis? I usually go every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received dialysis today before admission, and you’re scheduled again for Thursday. We’ll keep to your usual schedule. We’re also watching your fluid and potassium closely—so you’re on a 1.5-liter fluid limit and low-potassium diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’m used to it. But will I be able to breathe okay during surgery? I have sleep apnea and use oxygen at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You’ll continue your home oxygen during your stay. The anesthesia team knows about your sleep apnea and will monitor you closely. You’ll also be on supplemental oxygen after surgery until we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a little better knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today is the day for your wire localization. You’ll go to radiology first, where they’ll place two small wires to mark the exact spots of the masses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll use local anesthesia, so you’ll be awake but numb in the area. It might feel like pressure, but not sharp pain. Once the wires are in, you’ll go straight to surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the surgery—what exactly will they do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a wire-localized partial mastectomy. The surgeon will remove the tissue around each wire, including the masses, and also do a ‘global re-excision’ to make sure the margins are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Margins clear? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means no cancer cells at the edge of the removed tissue. That’s a good sign—shows we got it all. If not, we might need more surgery later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it’s clear. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did great. The surgery is over. You’re in recovery now. The procedure went smoothly, and you tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. Was everything removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both masses were successfully removed. The specimen x-ray confirmed the lesions were taken out with the wires. You’ll have a drain in place for a few days to prevent fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the heparin? Is that stopped now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped the heparin about 10 hours before surgery and restarted it 10 hours after. It’s running again now. We’ll keep it going until your INR is back in the therapeutic range on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m on a lot of meds—will they all go back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your home medications adjusted for dialysis. Omeprazole, amiodarone, paroxetine, insulin—all are being given as usual. We’re watching your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit sore, but okay. The drain is uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on the output. Once it drops below 30cc per day, we can remove it. Any fever, chills, or redness around the site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show mild anemia—hemoglobin is 8.8, which is expected with your kidney disease. We’re not giving a transfusion unless it drops further. You’re also on nephrocaps and Sensipar for bone and mineral balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take those at home. And I have that fungal rash on my sacrum from the last stay—any chance it came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse checked this morning—no rash now. We’re keeping the area clean and dry. You’re on contact isolation because of past MRSA and VRE, but you’re not infected now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we got an update from pathology. The final report shows multifocal invasive ductal carcinoma—two tumors, 0.6cm and 1.2cm. But the margins are clear. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Invasive? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the cancer started in the milk ducts and spread a small amount into surrounding tissue. But because it’s small and the margins are clear, surgery may be all you need. Oncology will review and let us know if you need chemo or radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So I might not need more treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly not. It depends on hormone receptor status and other markers, which are still pending. But right now, we’re optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your drain output is down to 25cc today. We’ll remove it tomorrow if it stays low. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I only took acetaminophen once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re also doing well on the diabetic, low-sodium diet. Blood pressure and glucose are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have dialysis today, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re scheduled for hemodialysis this afternoon. We’ll make sure the access site is clean and the team knows about your recent surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The drain is out, and the incision looks great—no signs of infection. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll need someone to help you at home for a few days. No lifting more than 5 pounds for at least two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister can stay with me. What about my Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on Coumadin at 5mg daily. Your INR was 2.6 this morning—perfect. Keep taking it at the same time every day, and avoid foods high in vitamin K.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like spinach and kale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll send you home with a list of foods to limit. Also, continue your insulin, omeprazole, and constipation meds—senna and MiraLAX—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. Dialysis went well yesterday. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need to see anyone after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll follow up with your surgeon in one week. Oncology will contact you about next steps. Also, keep your regular appointments with nephrology, primary care, and dermatology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis continues as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to your normal schedule. Call your doctor if you have fever, increased pain, redness, or drainage from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, morbid obesity, chronic diastolic heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and a history of venous thrombosis was admitted for surgical management of a right breast mass. She had a history of an enlarging breast lesion concerning for cancer, with recent imaging showing growth from 9mm to 14mm. Preoperatively, she was bridged from warfarin to heparin due to her anticoagulation needs. She underwent ultrasound-guided wire localization followed by a wire-localized right partial mastectomy with global re-excision. The procedure was successful, with final pathology revealing multifocal invasive ductal carcinoma, 0.6cm and 1.2cm, with clear margins. She tolerated the surgery well, remained on her home medications adjusted for dialysis, and completed two hemodialysis sessions during admission. The drain was removed on hospital day 5, and she was discharged home with plans for surgical and oncology follow-up, ongoing dialysis, and continuation of her chronic disease management.
